# Results — Study 280 (Solar-Eclipse) on the ^GSPC daily tape

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). Solar-eclipse dates,
types and US-path flags are hardcoded in [`data.py`](../solar_eclipse/data.py)
(central eclipses, 1928 onward). ^GSPC daily close-to-close price returns are from
the repo-level cache (`_cache/^GSPC_split_only.parquet`). Match the fingerprint
below to confirm you hold the same data. As-of **2026-06-17**.*

## Data stamp

| Source | Window | n observations | Fingerprint |
|---|---|---|---|
| ^GSPC daily (split-adjusted close, price-only) | 1928-01-03 – 2026-06-12 | 24,728 daily returns | `2fa7d20bebfd` |
| Solar-eclipse table | central eclipses 1930–2026 | 81 eclipses (80 in window) | hardcoded constant |

Survivorship note: ^GSPC is the index itself, so there is no constituent
survivorship bias — but it is **price-only** (no dividends) and the daily mean
drift is the honest baseline below.

## Event-study design

For each eclipse, **event day 0** is the first ^GSPC trading day on/after the
eclipse date (one built-in execution-lag day — the soonest a trader could act).
The **abnormal return** is the event-day return minus the full-sample daily mean
(`uncond = 3.16 bps/day`). We test the mean abnormal return with a Newey-West
(HAC, 3 lag) t-stat and a permutation test (10,000 random-day resamples, same n).

## Headline: do eclipses spook the market?

| Slice | n | mean abnormal (bps) | HAC t | perm p |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **All eclipses** | 80 | **+13.3** | **+1.12** | **0.307** |
| Total only | 57 | +6.9 | +0.50 | 0.647 |
| Annular only | 18 | +69.4 | +3.20 | 0.020 |
| US-path only (Great American etc.) | 12 | −11.8 | −0.28 | 0.696 |

- The headline (all 80 eclipses) shows an abnormal return of **+13 bps** on the
  eclipse trading day — the *wrong sign* for "spook" (eclipse days are mildly
  **positive**), and statistically a non-event: HAC t = **+1.12**, permutation
  p = **0.31**. Eclipse-day win rate is **62.5%** vs the ~54% unconditional
  up-day rate — again, not a swoon.
- The famous **US-path** eclipses (the 2017 and 2024 "Great American" totals and
  9 others) average **−11.8 bps** with t = **−0.28** — a shrug, not a crash.
- The 11-day CAR window (−5..+5) sums to **−56.7 bps**, dominated by pre-event
  days (−2, −1) and statistically indistinguishable from a random 11-day drift.

## The multiple-comparisons trap (why the "annular" slice is a mirage)

The **annular-only** slice looks significant raw (perm p = 0.020, HAC t = 3.20),
driven by two large up-days (1933-02-24 +3.9%, 2012-05-20 +1.6%). But we tested
**four** slices on the same tape. Bonferroni-correcting for 4 simultaneous tests:

| Slice | perm p | Bonferroni perm p |
|---|--:|--:|
| all eclipses | 0.307 | 1.00 |
| total only | 0.647 | 1.00 |
| annular only | 0.020 | **0.080** |
| US-path only | 0.696 | 1.00 |

After correction nothing clears 0.05. The "annular effect" is exactly the kind of
slice-until-it-sparkles artifact this desk exists to expose — there is no
mechanism by which the *shadow geometry* of an eclipse (annular vs total) would
move US equities.

## The tiny-n / tiny-effect problem

With ~80 eclipse days and ~1% daily ^GSPC volatility, the standard error on the
event-day mean is roughly `1% / sqrt(80) ≈ 11 bps`. To clear |t| = 2 the abnormal
return would need to exceed ~22 bps consistently; the observed +13 bps is below
that even before accounting for the four slices we searched.

## Positive control

On a synthetic daily tape with a planted eclipse-day **drag** the engine recovers
it cleanly (n_permutations = 1,000, seed = 280):

| planted (bps) | recovered mean abn (bps) | HAC t | perm p |
|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 0 | +9.4 | +0.84 | 0.40 |
| −50 | −40.5 | −3.64 | 0.000 |
| −150 | −140.2 | −12.6 | 0.000 |
| −300 | −289.7 | −26.1 | 0.000 |

The machinery detects a real effect when one exists; the real tape has nothing
like it.

## Could you trade it?

There is no tradable implementation. The signal fires a handful of times per
decade (two US-path eclipses in the entire 2010s), once per eclipse, for a single
day. A long/flat or long/short "eclipse-day" overlay pays one-way costs on every
turn (shorts also pay borrow), captures a noise-level +13 bps gross, and is
dominated by simply staying invested. Gross ≈ net only because there is no edge
to erode.

## Verdict

- **Signal — NONE.** All-eclipse abnormal return +13 bps, HAC t = +1.12,
  perm p = 0.31 — the *wrong sign* for the folklore and not significant. No slice
  survives multiple-comparisons correction. n is too small to detect anything
  below ~25 bps.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** No vehicle: a once-per-eclipse, single-day overlay
  with trading costs is dominated by passive buy-and-hold; there is no edge to
  monetise.
- **Busted — an omen that isn't.** Eclipses have been blamed for market panics
  since antiquity, but on 98 years of ^GSPC data the eclipse trading day is, if
  anything, mildly *up* — indistinguishable from any other day.
